'''David Leigh Donoho''' (born March 5, 1957) is an American statistician. He is a professor of statistics at [[Stanford University]], where he is also the Anne T. and [[Robert Bass (businessman)|Robert M. Bass]] Professor in the Humanities and Sciences.<ref name="chi"/> His work includes the development of effective methods for the construction of low-dimensional representations for high-dimensional data problems ([[multiscale geometric analysis]]), development of [[wavelets]] for denoising and [[compressed sensing]]. He was elected a Member of the [[American Philosophical Society]] in 2019.

==Academic biography==
Donoho did his undergraduate studies at [[Princeton University]], graduating in 1978.<ref name="bass"/> His undergraduate thesis advisor was [[John W. Tukey]].<ref name=AMS>{{cite web|title=2010 Norbert Wiener Prize|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/201004/rtx100400519p.pdf|publisher=American Mathematical Society|access-date=July 2, 2012}}</ref> Donoho obtained his Ph.D. from [[Harvard University]] in 1983, under the supervision of [[Peter J. Huber]].<ref name="mg">{{Mathgenealogy|name=David Leigh Donoho|id=18642}}.</ref> He was on the faculty of the [[University of California, Berkeley]], from 1984 to 1990 before moving to Stanford.

He has been the Ph.D. advisor of at least 20 doctoral students, including [[Jianqing Fan]] and [[Emmanuel Candès]].<ref name="mg"/>

==Awards and honors==
In 1991, Donoho was named a [[MacArthur Fellows Program|MacArthur Fellow]].<ref>{{citation|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1991/06/18/us/newark-priest-wins-a-genius-award.html|title=Newark Priest Wins a 'Genius' Award|journal=[[The New York Times]]|date=June 18, 1991|first=Kathleen|last=Teltsch}}.</ref> He was elected a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1992.<ref name=AAAS>{{cite web|title=Book of Members, 1780–2010: Chapter D|url=http://www.amacad.org/publications/BookofMembers/ChapterD.pdf|publisher=American Academy of Arts and Sciences|access-date=April 7, 2011}}</ref> He was the winner of the [[COPSS Presidents' Award]] in 1994. In 2001, he won the John von Neumann Prize of the [[Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics]].<ref>[http://www.siam.org/prizes/sponsored/vonneumann.php The John von Neumann Lecture], [[Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics|SIAM]], retrieved February 9, 2010.</ref> In 2002, he was appointed to the Bass professorship.<ref name="bass">[http://news.stanford.edu/news/2002/may29/endoweds-529.html Twelve professors honored with appointments to endowed chairs], Stanford Report, May 29, 2002.</ref> He was elected a [[Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics|SIAM]] Fellow<ref>[http://fellows.siam.org/index.php?sort=year&value=2009#David_Leigh_Donoho SIAM Fellows], retrieved February 9, 2010.</ref> and a foreign associate of the French [[Académie des sciences]]<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.academie-sciences.fr/actualites/communiques/communiques_html/elections_2009.htm |title=Actualités 2009 à l'Académie des Sciences |access-date=February 10, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100504053105/http://www.academie-sciences.fr/actualites/communiques/communiques_html/elections_2009.htm |archive-date=May 4, 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref> in 2009, and in the same year received an honorary doctorate from the [[University of Chicago]].<ref name="chi">[http://magazine.amstat.org/2009/12/donohodec09/ David L. Donoho Receives Honorary Degree], AMSTAT News, [[American Statistical Association]], December 1, 2009.</ref> In 2010 he won the [[Norbert Wiener Prize in Applied Mathematics]], given jointly by SIAM and the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[https://www.ams.org/ams/press/wiener-2010.html David Donoho Receives 2010 AMS-SIAM Wiener Prize in Applied Mathematics], [[American Mathematical Society]], January 14, 2010.</ref> He is also a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="bass"/><ref>[http://www.claymath.org/fas/senior_scholars/Donoho/ Profile] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180710041817/http://www.claymath.org/fas/senior_scholars/Donoho/ |date=July 10, 2018 }} as a [[Clay Mathematics Institute]] Senior Scholar, retrieved February 9, 2010.</ref> In 2012 he became a fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society], retrieved November 10, 2012.</ref> In 2013 he was awarded the [[Shaw Prize]] for Mathematics.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.shawprize.org/en/shaw.php?tmp=3&twoid=94 |title=2013 – Shaw Laureates – The Shaw Prize |access-date=July 9, 2013 |archive-date=July 10, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180710042057/http://www.shawprize.org/en/shaw.php?tmp=3&twoid=94 |url-status=dead }}</ref> In 2016, he was awarded an honorary degree at the [[University of Waterloo]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://uwaterloo.ca/registrar/convocation/honorary-and-award-recipients/fall-2016-honorary-and-award-recipients |title=- Fall 2016 honorary and award recipients – University of Waterloo |access-date=November 7, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161107224026/https://uwaterloo.ca/registrar/convocation/honorary-and-award-recipients/fall-2016-honorary-and-award-recipients |archive-date=November 7, 2016 |url-status=dead }}</ref> In 2018, he was awarded the Gauss Prize from IMU.
